title: What are the JPA cascade types (PERSIST, MERGE, REMOVE, DETACH, REFRESH, ALL), what does each do, and how does cascade differ from orphan removal?
keyPoints: PERSIST: persisting the parent also persists new children reachable through the cascaded association.
MERGE: merging a detached parent also merges children, copying their detached state into managed instances.
REMOVE: removing the parent also removes its children, but only when the parent itself is deleted.
DETACH/REFRESH: detaching or refreshing the parent propagates to children, useful for graph-level operations.
ALL is shorthand for PERSIST + MERGE + REMOVE + DETACH + REFRESH; use it for true aggregates where children are fully owned.
orphanRemoval deletes a child when it is removed from the collection, even while the parent lives on; REMOVE only fires when the parent is deleted.

s1_definition.oneliner: Cascade propagates parent operations (PERSIST/MERGE/REMOVE/DETACH/REFRESH, or ALL) to children; orphanRemoval deletes a child when it leaves the parent's collection.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **CascadeType.PERSIST** – persisting the parent also persists new children reachable through the association.
- **CascadeType.MERGE** – merging a detached parent also merges children, copying detached state into managed instances.
- **CascadeType.REMOVE** – removing the parent also removes its children; fires ONLY when the parent is deleted, not when a child is removed from the collection.
- **CascadeType.DETACH** – detaching the parent from the persistence context also detaches its children.
- **CascadeType.REFRESH** – refreshing the parent re-reads children from the database, discarding in-memory changes.
- **CascadeType.ALL** – shorthand for all five types; use for true aggregates where children have no life outside the parent.
- **orphanRemoval** – deletes a child when it is disassociated from the parent's collection, even while the parent lives on.
s1_definition.analogy: A customer (parent) at National Bank of India has orders (children). Cascade is the instruction: whatever I do to the customer, do the same to their orders. Save the customer and PERSIST cascades the new orders. Update a detached customer and MERGE cascades the updates. Close the customer account and REMOVE cascades to delete their orders. Orphan removal is a different, sharper rule: if I tear one order slip out of the customer's folder, shred that one slip, even though the customer still exists.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Cascade Types
  ============================================

  em.persist(parent)    -> CascadeType.PERSIST  -> persist children
  em.merge(parent)      -> CascadeType.MERGE    -> merge children
  em.remove(parent)     -> CascadeType.REMOVE   -> remove children
  em.detach(parent)     -> CascadeType.DETACH   -> detach children
  em.refresh(parent)    -> CascadeType.REFRESH  -> refresh children

  CascadeType.ALL = all five combined

  CASCADE REMOVE vs orphanRemoval
  ============================================

  em.remove(user):
    CASCADE REMOVE:    DELETE orders, DELETE user     (both fire)
    orphanRemoval:     DELETE orders, DELETE user     (both fire)

  user.getOrders().remove(order):
    CASCADE REMOVE:    nothing happens                (not triggered)
    orphanRemoval:     DELETE that order              (fires!)

  Key difference:
  CASCADE REMOVE  = parent deletion cascades
  orphanRemoval   = child disassociation deletes
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Cascade controls whether an operation on a parent entity automatically propagates to its associated children. PERSIST saves new children when the parent is saved. MERGE copies detached children state when the parent is merged. REMOVE deletes children when the parent is deleted. DETACH and REFRESH propagate detaching and re-reading across the graph. ALL is shorthand for all five, and Rajesh uses it for true aggregates at National Bank of India where orders have no life outside their user.

The distinction interviewers probe is cascade REMOVE versus orphan removal. Cascade REMOVE deletes children only when the parent itself is deleted. Orphan removal deletes a child the moment it is removed from the parent's collection, even while the parent continues to exist. Both mechanisms together give the complete aggregate lifecycle: creating, updating, deleting the whole user graph, and cancelling individual orders.

The senior cautions Pankaj gives are that cascade follows the object graph, so applying REMOVE or ALL to shared reference data is dangerous. He also remembers that cascade applies to EntityManager lifecycle operations and is completely bypassed by bulk JPQL DELETE statements, and that JPA cascade is a separate mechanism from a database-level ON DELETE CASCADE foreign key.

Remember one sentence: cascade propagates parent lifecycle operations to children, orphanRemoval deletes children removed from the collection, and both should only be applied to genuinely owned children.
